issues.legal_issue: A rent-based exclusion from rent-control protection does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality when it bears a rational relationship to the legislation’s objectives.
material_facts: The amended law excluded premises, residential or otherwise, when their monthly rent exceeded a specified threshold.

Reports and recommendations before the Legislature identified adverse effects of rent control, including reduced investment in rental housing, deterioration of housing stock, shortages of accommodation, and hardship to landlords.
The amendment aimed to balance landlords’ and tenants’ interests, encourage house building, and address problems created by the existing rent-control regime.
The Legislature chose a rent-based classification after considering a different proposed threshold.
Appellants argued that the classification ignored differences between residential and commercial premises, locations, sizes, tenants, and public or private occupants.
issues.conclusion: The rent-based classification was not shown to be irrational or unrelated to the amendment’s objectives and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: The constitutional guarantee of equality permits economic classifications that have an intelligible basis and a rational relationship to the statutory objective; courts allow the Legislature latitude in drawing classifications and selecting cut-offs and do not act as a super-legislature. A classification is invalid when it is wholly arbitrary or bears no nexus to the objective. The Court applied this approach under Article 14, relying on Harmon Singh v. Regional Transport Authority, City of New Orleans v. Dukes, Raval & Co. v. K.C. Ramachandra, Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu, Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Delhi Cloth & General Mills Ltd. v. S. Paramjit Singh, and Kerala Hotel & Restaurant Association v. State of Kerala. It distinguished Rattan Arya because that case concerned unequal treatment of residential and non-residential premises under a statute whose emphasized purpose was protecting weaker tenants.

rule.if: rent_control_classification_challenge and rent_value_classification and legislative_object_includes_balancing_interests and evidence_of_rent_control_harms

predicates.rent_control_classification_challenge: A party challenges an exclusion from rent-control protection on the ground that the classification is unequal.
predicates.rent_value_classification: The law distinguishes premises for rent-control coverage by the rent payable for them.
predicates.legislative_object_includes_balancing_in: The stated purpose of the legislation includes balancing the interests of landlords and tenants.
predicates.evidence_of_rent_control_harms: Reports or other material before the lawmaker identify harms attributed to the existing rent-control regime.

issues.definition: When an equality challenge concerns a rent-value classification, and the stated purpose includes balancing interests while material identifies harms from the existing regime, the classification is treated as valid under equality review.

issues.legal_issue: Removing statutory rent-control protection for premises above a rent threshold applies to tenancies that already existed when the change took effect.
material_facts: The amendment removed rent-control protection for premises whose monthly rent exceeded the specified threshold.
Some tenants argued that their earlier statutory protection was a vested right that could not be removed without express retrospective language.
The Court treated the amendment as a partial repeal that withdrew statutory protection from the affected category of tenants.
The premises at issue could already have been let when the amendment took effect.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion applies to premises already let when the amendment took effect if their monthly rent then exceeded the threshold; the Court did not express an opinion on its application to cases already pending in court.
issues.legal_principle: A tenant’s statutory protection exists while the statute applies, but the tenant does not acquire a vested right to have that statutory regime continue unchanged. A legislature may curtail or remove such protection, leaving the parties to the otherwise applicable law. The Court relied on Kay v. Goodwin, Kewal Singh v. Smt. Lajwanti, and Mohinder Kumar v. State of Haryana. It also distinguished acquired rights from a mere right to take advantage of a statute while it remains in force.

rule.if: rent_control_exemption_case and tenancy_existed_when_change_took_effect and rent_exceeded_threshold_then and protection_depended_on_continued_statutory_coverage

predicates.rent_control_exemption_case: The proceeding concerns whether a change to rent-control coverage removes protection from a tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_existed_when_change_took_effect: The premises had already been let when the change in the law took effect.
predicates.rent_exceeded_threshold_then: The monthly rent for the premises exceeded the applicable threshold when the change took effect.
predicates.protection_depended_on_continued_statuto: The tenant’s claimed protection arose from the statute rather than from an independently acquired right to continuation of that statutory regime.

issues.definition: For a rent-control coverage dispute, an existing tenancy whose rent exceeded the threshold when the change took effect loses the statutory protection that depended on continued coverage.

issues.legal_issue: For deciding whether premises exceed the rent threshold for rent-control coverage, rent means the rent actually paid rather than standard rent.
material_facts: The law excluded premises whose monthly rent exceeded a specified amount but did not use the term “standard rent” in the exclusion.
The law separately defined standard rent and provided a process for determining it.
The Court considered the amount of monthly rent being paid on the date the exclusion took effect to be the relevant measure.
The tenants argued that standard rent had to be determined before the exclusion could apply.
issues.conclusion: The relevant measure is the monthly rent actually being paid on the relevant date; prior determination of standard rent is not a precondition to applying the exclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Statutory words ordinarily bear their ordinary meaning. Where the exclusion refers to monthly rent and does not specify standard rent, the rent actually being paid is used to determine whether the premises fall within the excluded category; no prior standard-rent determination is required.

predicates.rent_threshold_coverage_case: The proceeding concerns whether premises fall within or outside rent-control coverage under a rent threshold.
predicates.statutory_text_uses_monthly_rent_without: The relevant text refers to monthly rent but does not state that standard rent is the measure.
predicates.actual_monthly_rent_exceeds_threshold: The monthly rent actually being paid for the premises exceeds the applicable threshold on the relevant date.

issues.definition: When a rent-threshold coverage dispute involves text referring to monthly rent without specifying standard rent, premises whose actual monthly rent exceeds the threshold are assessed by that actual rent.
